cues.en: In this lecture, we want to have a look at how do processors work.
This lecture is important because it will give us an important overview how all of those fits together
on our Linux machine, how all of this works together.
So let's have a look.
So a process, we can imagine it that this is an instance of a program.
This program may be an actual program that we launched, but it may also be a program that's running
in the background or a program that it's just helping out another program, but a process.
It's an instance of a program.
We can see a process as an independent execution unit with its own resources.
So, for example, a process gets signed, a certain amount of CPU time or memory resources that it
then can use, or the operating system decides on the fly how much processing power it wants to give
to a certain process.
But from the viewpoint of a process, it then knows, okay, this is the memory that I'm able to access
and oh, here I've just been assigned a certain amount of CPU time, so now I can do my computations.
So from the viewpoint of a process, it has its own CPU and memory resources.
They are not shared.
It also has its own resources in the sense that it has its own opened files and network connections
and all of that kind of stuff.
So we can really see it as an independent execution unit that has its own resources.
More on this and how we can still run multiple programs at the same time.
In a later lecture in this chapter, a process is managed by the kernel.
The kernel is the lowest level of the operating system.
We can imagine it as like a layer between our application code and the physical hardware, and the kernel
takes care of managing our process and assigning resources to it.
So for example, how much CPU time do we want to give to that process?
How much memory do we want to give to this process?
If the process asks for more memory, what do we do?
Do we just deny it or do we grant this additional resources but we just kill other apps that might be
running in the background?
That's what your phone is doing a lot actually.
So the kernel is managing the resources that are available to a process.
Each process has a so called process ID, that's the identifier for that process, also managed by the
operating system, which process ID it will get.
It also has a user under which this process runs under.
It has a state.
So usually it would be running, but it could also be waiting for something or it could be stopped or
it could be a zombie process.
We will have a more in-depth look at those process states in a later lecture here in this course and
various other properties that define this process.
All those processes are organized in a hierarchy and well, actually, let's just have a look at a practical
example.
So now I'm here on a Linux machine.
I just log in and we are here.
Let's say I start my Firefox here, what's doing or what's happening in the background that I'm now
able to have my Firefox here.
Let's have a look at the activity.
So there's a program here, it's called System Monitor here on my machine.
It might also be called Activity monitor or anything like this.
And here this is how it looks like currently, but it may look differently.
I've made the experience that those applications like to get updated a lot.
So if it looks different, that's totally all right as well.
But this is how it looks on my machine.
We can see that there are several processes here running on my machine and let's see if we can find
the Firefox.
I can just type it in and then we can see that there's Firefox running here.
We can see how much memory it's currently using, how much it's reading from the disk.
It has a process ID so we can see all of those properties that I was talking about.
We can also see that it's running under a specific user that defines the rights that this process has.
And we can see also, for example, here, additional properties about this process.
You remember that I was telling you that the processes are organized in a hierarchy.
We can see this here.
I have to go into the settings and here it's not called hierarchy, it's not called parent, It's called
show dependencies.
I can tick this checkbox and then we get a tree here that we can open and close.
But in order to actually see all the processes, we don't want to limit it by our users.
We want to show all the processes of all users.
So I click this box here, all processes and show dependencies.
Now we can see the process tree here and we can see here that for example, my gnome shell has opened
the Firefox browser that I'm using right now.
So we can see that we have a parent process here and then this process has started this process and
Firefox then has another process called web content, probably responsible for displaying this content
here.
So we can see this structure here, how this works internally.
Each process has another attribute that's called parent ID.
So for example here, if I would go into the properties, we could see that this process now, this
is the normal ID, um, it should have a parent ID somewhere.
It's actually not showing here.
Um, um, but at least we can see how it, how it's organizing this here as a tree structure.
But it works by this, that this process here, for example, will have the parent ID of 5590 and 5590
would be the Firefox and this process would have the parent ID of 1910, which would be the gnome shell.
So we can see how all of this here works together.
Let's say I start a terminal here, so I open another app here, for example, the terminal.
And now let's see what's happening here.
If I would now be in a terminal here, we can see here that we have this terminal server that's probably
this app.
But let's see how how that works.
I keep this here and now let's just start another process here in my terminal.
So for example, here in my terminal, I could start another bash.
So now we are in a shell.
In a shell or inside that one I could start with a pink command, for example, to ping the server of
Google.com 100 times.
And now you can see here that we are sending those packets and we are sending 100 packets here.
It's not happening here.
So probably I need to look for another process.
Let's see where my ping is.
It's actually in the terminal server.
The way it works here is that now everything is filtered and I need to remove that filter and then scroll
to the corresponding position to see all the processes.
So now you can see here we have this terminal server inside, we have our first bash.
Then you remember I started yet another bash inside that one and then another and then the ping command
inside that bash.
So this is how it works here.
And you can see that we are having this process hierarchy here that is doing all the work here on our
system.
And yeah, this is how all of our system here works.
So now that we have been able to get a quick overview over our processes, how do we solve it if we
are not able to use a GUI or a nice user interface to get to this list?
So what do we do if we only have command line access to a system?
And for that I want to introduce you to the PS command which will allow you to browse those processes
from the command line.
But we'll have a look at that in the next lecture.
